cues.en: I'm going show you a very interesting test of perfect pitch, your ability to identify a note without a reference. I'm going play you two notes and I'm going ask you a question. Ready? Okay. Here's note one
cues.zh: 我要给你们看一个非常有趣的绝对音感测试，也就是在没有参照音的情况下辨认音高的能力。我会弹两个音，然后问你们一个问题。准备好了吗？好，这是第一个音。

cues.en: and here's note two.
cues.zh: 这是第二个音。

cues.en: So my question for you is this,
cues.zh: 那么我的问题是：

cues.en: which of these two notes was higher than the other?
cues.zh: 这两个音里，哪一个比另一个更高？

cues.en: This question sounds simple, but statistically speaking, if you have perfect pitch, you are less likely to get this question correct than people like me who don't have perfect pitch because you're perceiving the pitch chroma, the name of the note, more readily than the relationship between the notes.
cues.zh: 这个问题听起来很简单，但从统计上看，如果你有绝对音感，你答对这道题的概率反而比像我这样没有绝对音感的人更低，因为你会更容易感知到音高色度，也就是音名，而不是两个音之间的关系。

cues.en: It's very interesting. Here's another one. I'm gonna play you two melodies.
cues.zh: 这很有意思。再来看一个。我放两段旋律给你听。

cues.en: This is melody one
cues.zh: 这是旋律一

cues.en: and melody two.
cues.zh: 这是旋律二。

cues.en: Even though the melody start on different notes, the distances between the notes is the same, and so we think of them as being the same melody just transposed to different keys. But that isn't as immediately obvious to people with perfect pitch. There is a 2002 study where musicians with perfect pitch and without perfect pitch were shown sheet music of a melody and then played that melody back in a different key.
cues.zh: 尽管这两段旋律从不同的音符开始，但音符之间的距离是一样的，所以我们认为它们是同一段旋律，只是移到了不同的调。但对有绝对音感的人来说，这并不那么一目了然。2002年有一项研究：让有绝对音感和没有绝对音感的音乐家看一段旋律的乐谱，然后用不同的调把这段旋律演奏出来。

cues.en: They were then asked if the sheet music was the same melody as what they were hearing. Is this the same melody? And if it isn't the same melody, where does the melody change? Musicians with perfect pitch fared worse at perceiving the transpositional identity of the same melody
cues.zh: 然后他们被问到，这份乐谱和他们听到的是不是同一段旋律。这是同一段旋律吗？如果不是同一段旋律，旋律是在哪里变的？有绝对音感的音乐家在感知同一旋律的移调同一性时，表现反而更差

cues.en: than musicians without perfect pitch.
cues.zh: 比没有绝对音感的音乐家。

cues.en: Very interesting. Now don't get me wrong. There are many things that people with perfect pitch can do that I can't, and I am definitely jealous of what folks like June Lee and Jacob Collier can do with their superhuman feats of ear training.
cues.zh: 非常有意思。别误会我。有绝对音感的人能做很多我做不到的事，而且我绝对羡慕像 June Lee 和 Jacob Collier 这样的人在听觉训练上展现出的超人本领。

cues.en: But there are some reasons why you might not want to have perfect pitch, and your life as a musician or music lover is better without it.
cues.zh: 但有些原因会让你可能不想拥有完美音高，而且作为音乐人或音乐爱好者，没有它你的生活反而更好。

cues.en: Let's get into them.
cues.zh: 我们来聊聊这些原因。

cues.en: This video is brought to you by Curiosity Stream and my streaming service, Nebula.
cues.zh: 本视频由 Curiosity Stream 和我的流媒体服务 Nebula 赞助。

cues.en: Perfect pitch, or technically absolute pitch, is a
cues.zh: 完美音高，或者从技术上说，绝对音感，是一种

cues.en: disease. We're here with Charlie Pooh. Charlie has a really crazy talent. He has a disease that's called perfect pitch. And basically can hear notes and he knows what they are just by listening to them. It's hard to know just how many people are afflicted by the malady.
cues.zh: 病。我们请到了 Charlie Pooh。Charlie 有个非常离谱的天赋。他得了一种叫完美音高的病。基本上，他能听出音符，光靠听就知道是什么音。很难知道到底有多少人受这种病困扰。

cues.en: Some studies suggest that it's just one in ten thousand,
cues.zh: 有些研究表明，它只有万分之一，

cues.en: but the noted epidemiologist
cues.zh: 但著名流行病学家

cues.en: Jimmy Fallon pegs that number a little bit higher. Do know what that is? Perfect pitch. Like, less than one percent of us have this talent. And my YouTube algorithm breaking poll pegs that number at 3%,
cues.zh: Jimmy Fallon 把这个数字估得稍高一点。知道那是什么吗？完美音高。大概不到 1% 的人有这种天赋。而我在 YouTube 上那个“搞崩算法”的投票，把这个数字定在 3%，

cues.en: which is a lot higher than one in 10,000. So what exactly is going on here?
cues.zh: 这比万分之一高多了。那这到底是怎么回事？

cues.en: Picture perception exists kind of on a gradient from
cues.zh: 音高感知有点像一段渐变，从

cues.en: I have no idea what's going on to...
cues.zh: “我完全不知道怎么回事”到……

cues.en: You
cues.zh: 你

cues.en: can kind of think of four categories here. Untrained,
cues.zh: 这里可以大致分成四类。未训练音高，

cues.en: relative pitch, quasi absolute pitch, and absolute pitch. And the way that we're gonna talk about this is in terms of color perception because that's often how people with absolute pitch think of it as pitch chroma, pitch color. Untrained pitch is when you just don't categorize pitch when you're listening to music. It's like seeing the world in black and white. You might have a very deep relationship to the objects in the scene, the apple tastes just as fine to you, but you aren't perceiving
cues.zh: 相对音高、准绝对音高和绝对音高。我们讨论的方式是用颜色感知，因为绝对音高的人通常把它理解为音高色度、音高色彩。未训练的音高，就是你听音乐时完全不把音高分类。就像看黑白世界。你可能对场景中的物体有很深的联结，苹果对你来说一样好吃，但你并没有感知到

cues.en: the pitch. Absolute pitch is like seeing the world in color. You don't have to think about whether or not the apple is red, it's just red.
cues.zh: 音高。绝对音高就像看到彩色世界。你不用去想苹果是不是红的，它就是红的。

cues.en: The plant is green.
cues.zh: 植物是绿色的。

cues.en: The note is f sharp. With true absolute pitch, there is no thought process and no reference.
cues.zh: 这个音是升F。拥有真正的绝对音感时，没有思考过程，也不需要参照。

cues.en: The current scientific thinking suggests that the encoding occurs very early on in auditory perception. People who speak tonal languages like Mandarin,
cues.zh: 目前的科学观点认为，这种编码发生在听觉感知的极早期。说声调语言（比如普通话）的人，

cues.en: where the pitch contour is very important in communicating information,
cues.zh: 而在这类语言里，音高轮廓对信息传达非常重要，

cues.en: are more likely to develop absolute pitch than people who don't natively speak tonal languages, as well as people who start their musical training very early on in life. A full 74%
cues.zh: 比母语不是声调语言的人，以及比很早就开始音乐训练的人，更有可能发展出绝对音感。高达74%

cues.en: of native Mandarin speakers who had their musical training start before age five had developed absolute pitch in one study, way more than that one in ten thousand number cited earlier. Now, I know this is controversial, but it's generally understood that you cannot learn perfect pitch as an adult. It is something that is learned in early childhood, and there's really nothing that you can do about it. But you can learn something which is almost as good and that is called quasi perfect pitch. Quasi absolute pitch is kind of like looking at this grayscale image and seeing the apple and then remembering, oh yeah, apples are red and then seeing color. It's not as immediate,
cues.zh: 的母语为普通话者中，五岁前开始接受音乐训练的人，在一项研究里发展出了绝对音感，远高于前面提到的万分之一这个数字。我知道这有争议，但普遍认为，成年后无法学会绝对音感。它是在幼儿时期学会的，对此你实在无能为力。但你可以学会一种几乎同样厉害的东西，叫作准绝对音感。准绝对音感有点像看着这张灰度图，认出苹果，然后想起来，哦对，苹果是红色的，然后才看到颜色。它没有那么直接，

cues.en: it's based on a memory but you can use that memory to your advantage. There's a couple of ways that this works. The first way is what's called true pitch or instrument specific absolute pitch. It's when you are so familiar with the timbre of a specific note on a specific instrument because you've played it over and over again. It's why many guitarists just know what the sound of the open e string of a guitar is.
cues.zh: 它建立在记忆之上，但你可以把这种记忆变成优势。这有几种方式。第一种叫真实音高，或乐器特定的绝对音高。它是指你对某件乐器上某个音的音色极其熟悉，因为你一遍又一遍地弹过它。这就是为什么很多吉他手一听就知道吉他空E弦的声音。

cues.en: It's... That's the open e string. Woodwind players, especially in my experience, clarinet players often have this because there's such a unique tone color to every note on the instrument and they become very familiar with those unique tone colors as they relate to pitch. This all adds up to the thought process of, hey, that's an apple and apples are red. There's also something called heightened tonal memory which affects both musicians and non musicians.
cues.zh: 这是……那是空弦 E 弦。木管乐手，尤其据我的经验，单簧管演奏者常有这种能力，因为乐器上每个音都有独特的音色，而他们会非常熟悉这些与音高相关的独特音色。这些汇总起来就是一种思维过程：嘿，那是苹果，苹果是红色的。还有一种叫增强音调记忆的现象，既影响音乐家，也影响非音乐家。

cues.en: Sometimes it's called the Leviton effect where you've heard a song so often before that you can always reproduce that song in the correct key. Honestly, you know what I go to? I go to a couple things. I go to Green Dolphin Street for one. Mhmm. So I always know where E... I know I always know where E Flat is. I go to the so what baseline.
cues.zh: 有时这被称为 Levitin 效应——一首歌你听过太多遍，就总能把它用正确的调重现出来。说实话，我会靠什么？我会靠几样东西。其中之一是 Green Dolphin Street。嗯哼。所以我总是知道降E在哪儿，我总是知道降E的位置。我会靠《So What》的贝斯线。

cues.en: So I always know where... That's a good one. Yeah. That's a real... And I go to an f blues.
cues.zh: 所以我总是知道……那个很好用。是啊，那是真正的……另外我会靠F布鲁斯。

cues.en: Interesting. Okay. Some people might think I have perfect pitch if I'm quick enough at picking out those anchor points using relative pitch to figure out whatever the note you just played was.
cues.zh: 有意思。好。如果我够快，能用相对音感找出那些锚点，推断出你刚弹的是什么音，有些人可能会以为我有绝对音感。

cues.en: But that's not what's happening. It's actually just... I'm I'm just bouncing it off of a memory
cues.zh: 但事实并非如此。其实只是……我只是拿一段记忆来对照

cues.en: that I have as like an anchor,
cues.zh: 那段记忆就像锚点，

cues.en: and then using relative pitch to to figure it out. Like for me, unfortunately,
cues.zh: 然后用相对音感推出来。对我来说，不幸的是，

cues.en: the song that the Leviton effect is most lodged in my brain is
cues.zh: Leviton 效应在我脑中扎根最深的那首歌是

cues.en: the last chorus
cues.zh: 最后一段副歌，

cues.en: to Don't Stop Believing by Journey.
cues.zh: 出自 Journey 的《Don't Stop Believing》。

cues.en: That's that's an e by the way, that truck. Because the last chorus of don't stop believing goes, don't
cues.zh: 顺便说一句，那是 E，那个和弦。因为《Don't Stop Believin'》最后一段副歌是：don't

cues.en: stop.
cues.zh: stop.

cues.en: Which
cues.zh: 这

cues.en: is an a and g sharp and then that's down to an e.
cues.zh: 是 A 和 G♯，然后下到 E。

cues.en: I'm not even gonna check.
cues.zh: 我甚至都懒得去查。

cues.en: But I don't have perfect pitch. I just have tonal memory
cues.zh: 但我没有绝对音感。我只是有音高记忆

cues.en: so deep in my brain because of cover gigs.
cues.zh: 因为跑翻唱演出，它在我脑子里扎得太深了。

cues.en: Relative pitch is the final category and it's probably the most useful for musicians. It's what we're trained in. It's the ability to identify notes and scales and chords and melodies and intervals and the relationships between them. So if you played this for a trained musician,
cues.zh: 相对音感是最后一类，而且对音乐家来说可能最有用。这正是我们受训的内容。它是识别音符、音阶、和弦、旋律、音程以及它们之间关系的能力。所以如果你把这段放给受过训练的音乐家听，

cues.en: they'd probably be able to tell you, oh yes, that's a two minor seven, a five seven flat nine, and a one major seven. They wouldn't necessarily be able to tell you the names of the notes, they could tell you the relationships between them so that if you gave a reference, like you said the first chord began on the note G, they could calculate out the rest of the notes in the rest of the chords. The implications of this are kind of weird when you apply the color analogy here. It's like seeing this image in grayscale
cues.zh: 他们大概能告诉你，哦对，那是一个二级小七、一个五级七降九，和一个一级大七。他们不一定能说出这些音符的名字，但能说出它们之间的关系；所以如果你给一个参照，比如你说第一个和弦从 G 音开始，他们就能推算出其余和弦里的其余音符。把颜色类比套到这里，其中的含义有点怪。就像把这张图看成灰度图。

cues.en: and then being told that the plant is green,
cues.zh: 然后被告知这株植物是绿色的，

cues.en: therefore the apple must be red.
cues.zh: 所以苹果一定是红色的。

cues.en: It's like you're perceiving the wavelengths of the green and then calculating out the redness of the apple.
cues.zh: 这就像你先感知到绿色对应的波长，再推算出苹果的红色。

cues.en: Having relative pitch is kind of like being color blind and then working out what colors are based on context. Color analogy breaks down a little bit here, but it's still kind of useful in understanding how other people might experience pitch.
cues.zh: 拥有相对音高有点像色盲，然后根据上下文推断出颜色。颜色类比在这里有点站不住脚，但它仍然有助于理解别人可能如何感知音高。

cues.en: You know, when you assign
cues.zh: 你知道，当你把

cues.en: words like red to some kind of color experience, you're assigning a category to that experience. It's called categorical perception.
cues.zh: 像“红”这样的词对应到某种颜色体验上时，你就是在给那种体验归入一个类别。这叫做范畴感知。

cues.en: And that categorical perception is very much dependent on the language with which you speak. So for example, in Russian,
cues.zh: 而这种范畴感知很大程度上取决于你说的语言。比如在俄语里，

cues.en: there are multiple words for what in English we might just call like blue.
cues.zh: 英语里我们可能只叫“蓝色”的东西，俄语里有好几个词。

cues.en: Like, there are multiple words for this.
cues.zh: 比如，这个就有好几个词。

cues.en: What's interesting is that studies of perfect pitch and absolute pitch have really just dealt with one kind of category
cues.zh: 有意思的是，关于完美音高和绝对音高的研究其实只涉及一种范畴，

cues.en: and that is 12 tone equal temperament. People who are trained in 12 tone equal temperament
cues.zh: 那就是十二平均律。受过十二平均律训练的人

cues.en: are more likely to assign their perception to the notes of the piano.
cues.zh: 更可能把自己的感知归到钢琴的音符上。

cues.en: I'd be really fascinated to see if that translates to different kinds of tuning systems and different cultures that didn't have 12 tone equal temperament as the default. But there haven't been any studies on that, so we shall see.
cues.zh: 我很想看看，这是否也适用于那些不以十二平均律为默认的不同音律体系和不同文化。但还没有相关研究，所以只能拭目以待。

cues.en: So to recap, have four ways of experiencing pitch. We have absolute pitch, we have quasi absolute pitch, we have relative pitch, and then we have the untrained ear. So with all that in mind, why possibly would a musician not want to have absolute pitch? Why wouldn't we wanna see the world in color? That seems strange.
cues.zh: 总结一下，体验音高有四种方式：绝对音高、准绝对音高、相对音高，以及未受训练的耳朵。既然如此，音乐家为什么可能不想要绝对音高呢？我们为什么不想看到彩色的世界呢？这似乎很奇怪。

cues.en: Well, I have some unfortunate news for the people with perfect pitch watching this video, and it comes from the great concert pianist,
cues.zh: 嗯，对正在看这个视频、拥有绝对音感的人，我有个坏消息，它来自伟大的钢琴演奏家，

cues.en: Abby Simon. If you have absolute pitch, perfect pitch,
cues.zh: Abby Simon。如果你有绝对音感，也就是完美音高，

cues.en: if you live long enough, you will lose it. Rick Beato did a video recently on people who lose their perfect pitch. And it seems to be that this is something that happens universally
cues.zh: 如果你活得够久，就会失去它。Rick Beato 最近做了一个关于失去绝对音感的人的视频。而且看起来，这是普遍会发生的事，

cues.en: across the board after a certain age. Like, you have it,
cues.zh: 过了某个年龄后，无一例外。就像，你拥有它，

cues.en: you only have a short window to enjoy it and use it before it goes away. So your perfect pitch has No.
cues.zh: 你只有很短的窗口期去享受和使用它，然后它就会消失。所以你的绝对音感，没了。

cues.en: It's it's it's gone down the tube with... A study from 2012 found that sixteen out of twenty people tested with absolute pitch over the age of 45
cues.zh: 它已经彻底不行了……2012年的一项研究发现，在45岁以上接受测试的20人中，有16人的绝对音高

cues.en: had their absolute pitch shifted
cues.zh: 发生了偏移

cues.en: by a semitone or more. This was corroborated by another study in 2016,
cues.zh: 偏移了一个半音甚至更多。2016年的另一项研究证实了这一点，

cues.en: which also found that this perfect pitch shift had nothing to do with the mechanical hearing loss that normally comes with aging. In the Society for Music Theory Listserv, researcher David Huron asked the question if there were any examples of people over the age of 60 who didn't experience this pitch shift.
cues.zh: 该研究还发现，这种绝对音高偏移与衰老通常带来的机械性听力损失无关。在音乐理论学会的Listserv上，研究者David Huron提出一个问题：是否有任何60岁以上的人没有经历这种音高偏移的例子。

cues.en: None were given. The great jazz vibraphonist,
cues.zh: 没有给出任何说明。伟大的爵士颤音琴演奏家，

cues.en: Gary Burton, has talked frequently about his loss of perfect pitch like on this interview from Adam Tan's YouTube channel. Well, was interesting. It was confusing. I lost the perfect pitch in 2011.
cues.zh: Gary Burton 经常谈到自己失去绝对音感，比如在 Adam Tan 的 YouTube 频道这段采访里。嗯，挺有意思。也很让人困惑。我在 2011 年失去了绝对音感。

cues.en: It was something I had gotten used to
cues.zh: 那曾是我已经习惯的东西

cues.en: and kinda depended on as a, you know, a sense of always kinda knowing where everything is. Suddenly discovered that, you know, that piece of information
cues.zh: 而且有点依赖它，你知道，就像一种总能大概知道每个音在哪儿的感觉。突然发现，你知道，那条信息

cues.en: was no longer available to me. In her master's thesis, Understanding and Dealing with the Loss of Absolute Pitch as One Ages, Mary L. Bianco catalogs correspondence with older musicians who have lost their absolute pitch. The experience was annoying,
cues.zh: 我已经再也无法获取了。Mary L. Bianco 在她的硕士论文《理解并应对随着年龄增长而失去绝对音感》中，整理了与失去绝对音感的年长音乐家的通信。这种经历很烦人，

cues.en: often getting in the way of my enjoyment of music. I'm sad to have lost something that felt very special to me. What was occurring was truly jolting to my sense of musicality
cues.zh: 常常妨碍我享受音乐。失去一个对我而言非常特别的东西，我很难过。当时发生的一切，确实强烈冲击了我的音乐感受。

cues.en: and my sense of self. Another account reads, around the time I got my first pair of reading glasses, my sense of absolute pitch started to waver. I got Cs and Bs mixed up, and to be honest, this was a surprisingly alarming development.
cues.zh: 以及我的自我认同感。另一段记述写道，大约在我戴上第一副老花镜的时候，我的绝对音感开始动摇。我会把 C 和 B 搞混，说实话，这个变化出乎意料地令人警觉。

cues.en: A whole dimension of my existence seemed to fade away. The thing to me that's most frightening about this is not just that the perfect pitch goes away, like you're now seeing the world in black and white when you used to see it in color.
